questions.stem: Which of the following salts is insoluble in water?
questions.explanation: Most sulphates dissolve, but barium and lead(II) sulphates are the standard exceptions. Barium sulphate is so insoluble that it is used as the white precipitate confirming the presence of sulphate ions in a test.

distractorRationale.a: All sodium salts are soluble, including the carbonate
distractorRationale.b: All trioxonitrates(V) without exception are soluble
distractorRationale.d: All ammonium salts are soluble

questions.stem: Sodium hydrogentetraoxosulphate(VI), NaHSO4, is classified as
questions.explanation: Tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid is dibasic, so it has two replaceable hydrogens. In NaHSO4 only one has been replaced by sodium, leaving a hydrogen that can still be donated. A salt that retains replaceable hydrogen is an acid salt.

distractorRationale.a: In a normal salt every replaceable hydrogen has been replaced, as in Na2SO4
distractorRationale.c: A basic salt contains hydroxide or oxide ions in addition to the acid anion
distractorRationale.d: A double salt is two simple salts crystallised together, such as potash alum

questions.stem: The most suitable method for preparing lead(II) chloride in the laboratory is

options.text: adding excess lead(II) oxide to dilute hydrochloric acid and filtering
titrating lead(II) hydroxide solution against hydrochloric acid
mixing solutions of lead(II) trioxonitrate(V) and sodium chloride, then filtering
adding lead metal to dilute hydrochloric acid

questions.explanation: Lead(II) chloride is insoluble, so it is made by precipitation. Two soluble salts are mixed, Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2NaCl(aq) -> PbCl2(s) + 2NaNO3(aq), and the white precipitate is filtered off, washed with distilled water and dried.

distractorRationale.a: Filtering would not separate the insoluble product from the unreacted excess oxide, since both are solids
distractorRationale.b: Lead(II) hydroxide is insoluble, so no solution exists to place in the burette
distractorRationale.d: Lead reacts extremely slowly with dilute hydrochloric acid, and the insoluble chloride coats the metal and stops the reaction

questions.stem: Copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) cannot be prepared by adding copper metal to dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid because copper

options.text: lies below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid
forms an insoluble sulphate that stops the reaction
reacts violently and dangerously with the acid

questions.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen in the activity series can displace hydrogen from a dilute acid. Copper is below hydrogen, so no reaction occurs. The salt is instead prepared from copper(II) oxide or copper(II) carbonate, which are bases and react with the acid readily.

distractorRationale.a: Hardness has no bearing on chemical reactivity; sodium is soft yet extremely reactive
distractorRationale.c: Copper(II) sulphate is in fact very soluble, which is why it can be crystallised from solution
distractorRationale.d: There is no reaction at all, so no violence is involved

questions.stem: Titration must be used rather than the excess-solid method when preparing sodium chloride from sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid because

options.text: sodium chloride is insoluble in water
sodium hydroxide is soluble, so any excess could not be filtered off
the reaction is too slow without a burette
hydrochloric acid is too weak to react with sodium hydroxide

questions.explanation: The excess-solid method works only because the leftover solid can be filtered out. Sodium hydroxide dissolves completely, so any excess would stay in the solution and contaminate the product. Titration establishes the exact volumes that react, and the experiment is then repeated without indicator.

distractorRationale.a: Sodium chloride is very soluble, which is precisely why it must be crystallised from solution
distractorRationale.c: Neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong alkali is essentially instantaneous
distractorRationale.d: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid and reacts readily with sodium hydroxide

questions.stem: All trioxonitrate(V) salts, commonly called nitrates, are soluble in water.
questions.explanation: True. Nitrates are the one anion group with no insoluble members at all, which is why nitrate solutions are the standard starting point for precipitation reactions. Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are similarly always soluble.

questions.stem: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate crystals should be dried between sheets of filter paper rather than in a hot oven because oven drying would

options.text: drive off the water of crystallisation and leave a white anhydrous powder
make the crystals absorb carbon dioxide from the air

questions.explanation: The blue colour belongs to the hydrated form, CuSO4.5H2O. Heating removes the five water molecules built into the crystal lattice, converting the blue crystals into white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate and destroying the product you set out to make.

distractorRationale.a: Heating dries rather than dissolves; dissolving needs added solvent
distractorRationale.c: Copper(III) is not formed under these conditions
distractorRationale.d: Copper(II) sulphate does not react with atmospheric carbon dioxide

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a normal salt?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is a normal salt because it is formed from the neutralization of a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH). Normal salts contain no replaceable hydrogen ions, unlike acid or basic salts.

distractorRationale.b: Calcium hydrogen carbonate is an acid salt due to the presence of replaceable hydrogen ions.
distractorRationale.c: Potassium dihydrogen phosphate is also an acid salt because it contains hydrogen ions that can be replaced.
distractorRationale.d: Copper(II) hydroxide is a basic salt, as it contains hydroxide ions that can react with acids.
